The couplet normally consists of a root having one of the following shapes: CVCV, CVV, VCV, VV. Stress is on the first (C)V. Since there are no couplets of the shape CVVCV or CVCCV ... there is some indeterminacy about whether the couplet should be referred to as consisting of two moras or two syllables. The couplet may be preceded or followed by monosyllabic morphemes which are dependent on the root. In this study, we shall refer to those which precede the root as proclitics and those which follow the root as enclitics. ... new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Peñoles Mixtec (catalog-all-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements, so this source supplies the placement outright: penultimate syllable of the (mostly disyllabic) morpheme, tonal language, optional stressed-syllable lengthening. It contradicts nothing.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (acento) falls on the penultimate syllable of every morpheme of two or more syllables; since most stems are disyllabic (the Mixtec couplet) this is the first syllable of the stem. Monosyllabic morphemes are clitics (written with a hyphen) and carry no stress of their own. The stressed syllable may optionally be realized with a lengthened vowel and/or lengthened following consonant. The language is tonal (high and low tones, plus modified high and low tones, p.25ff.), so stress is a separate, predictable property alongside lexical tone.
new_statements.exceptions: No exceptions stated. Trisyllabic morphemes exist (a few, loans or native, e.g. /andiu/ 'cielo', /ʃikwela/ 'escuela'); the penultimate rule covers them without comment. The domain is the morpheme, not the phonological word: stem + enclitic sequences such as /kiši-dé/ keep stress on the stem's penult.
new_statements.identity_note: All material concerns the Mixtec of Santa María Peñoles, Oaxaca (ISO mil, Glottolog peno1244), the variety John and Margaret Daly worked on; the ALIM 3 volume names the town explicitly in its title. No other dialect is described.

new_statements.quote: Other phonemes are high tone (´), low tone (unmarked), tone modification (`),5 and nasalization (˛). Stress is predictable in terms of morpheme syllable structure. It falls on the penultimate syllable of morphemes with two or more syllables (a syllable being an optional consonant, plus obligatory vowel, plus optional glottal catch). Morphemes of a single syllable are never stressed and are phonologically dependent on stressed morphemes. (The phonological dependence of monosyllabic morphemes is indicated by a hyphen at the beginning of a morpheme).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and computed on the morpheme: every morpheme of two or more syllables (the Mixtec root 'couplet', CV(ʔ) syllables) is stressed on its penultimate syllable, i.e. the first syllable of a disyllabic root; monosyllabic morphemes (proclitics/enclitics, written with a hyphen) are never stressed and lean on a stressed morpheme. The language is tonal (high, low, 'tone modification') and stress is stated independently of tone.
new_statements.exceptions: none; monosyllabic morphemes are categorically unstressed; morphemes of three syllables (implied by 'two or more') take penultimate stress
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern the Mixtec of Santa María Peñoles, Oaxaca (ISO mil, 'Peñoles Mixtec'; SIL archive subject language Peñoles Mixtec [mil]); Daly 1973 is by the same SIL fieldworker (John P. Daly) as the works already read.

new_statements.quote: The phonemes of Peñoles Mixtec, not including tone, are: voiceless stops /p t č k kw ʔ/, prenasalized stops /mb nd nǰ ngw/, voiceless fricatives /f s š h/, voiced fricatives /b d ž/, nasals /m n ñ/, liquids /l r/, vowels /i e ɨ a u o/, and nasalization. Stress occurs on the first syllable of disyllabic nouns. In the orthography employed here, enclitics are set off by hyphens.

It is consistent with the same author's Spanish description already held by the project from an earlier reading (Daly & Daly 1977, ALIM 3, p.19: 'El acento se localiza en la penúltima sílaba de los morfemas de dos o más sílabas'), which words the same fact as penult-of-morpheme.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the first syllable of a disyllabic noun (for a disyllable this is the penultimate syllable, i.e. the first syllable of the Mixtec root couplet); enclitics are written with hyphens and are outside the noun; stress is mentioned once, in a footnote, as non-tonal background to a tone analysis, and no contrastive function is attributed to it. The language is tonal (four tonemes argued for: high, modified high, low, modified low).
new_statements.exceptions: none for stress (the statement is restricted to disyllabic nouns; nothing is said about longer words, verbs, or clitic groups). Tone-rule exceptions are listed in note 7 but do not concern stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Daly's data are from Santa María Peñoles, Etla, Oaxaca (fieldwork from 1957; c. 2,000 speakers in the municipio plus c. 8,000 in ten other communities 'with dialect variation', p.17 n.1). The North & Shields chapter in the same volume describes Silacayoapan Mixtec, a different Mixtec language, and its couplet-initial stress statement (p.22) must not be attributed to Peñoles.

tone_statements.quote: Tone Bearing Units (TBUs) are syllables, and each can be H(igh), L(ow), or unspecified Ø. The evidence for underspecification is diverse. The specified tones H and L can form rising LH-contours, whereas Ø cannot form any contours. … Finally, the phonetic realisation of Ø is low-falling unless followed by H, in which case its pitch will match H. Neither the low-falling realisation nor the H anticipation are indicative of a phonological specification as M or another full-fledged tone.
tone_statements.summary: Syllable = TBU, each H, L or toneless Ø; rising LH contours are tone sequences; floating L docks rightward across words; OCP-L, H-tone spreading, floating-L deletion; data from Daly & Hyman 2007.

tone_statements.citation: Daly, John P. & Larry M. Hyman. 2007. On the representation of tone in Peñoles Mixtec. International Journal of American Linguistics 73(2): 165-207. PDF from linguistics.berkeley.edu/~hyman/papers/
tone_statements.quote: In PM, each V is an independent tone-bearing unit (TBU). However, not every TBU is underlyingly speciﬁed for tone. Rather, the analysis for which we present evidence in this study recognizes two underlying tones, /H/ and /L/ (high and low), which contrast with /W/ (absence of lexical tone). … For present purposes, sufﬁce it to say that /H/ varies between high and mid pitch, /L/ is realized on a level low pitch, and /W/ varies between level mid and falling low pitch.
tone_statements.locator: p. 167, sec. 2 'Lexical tone patterns'; downstep statement p. 184 sec. 4; floating L in abstract p. 165 and sec. 2 pp. 167-169
tone_statements.summary: Underlying high, low and toneless W ('three-value system'); each root vowel is H or W, the always-floating L links only to the stressed root-initial syllable; phonemic downstep and upstep of H.

tone_statements.quote: While the underlying system consists of a contrast between /H/, /L/ and /Ø/, pitch realization rules produce high-rising, low-falling, and mid output tones. … In PM each V is an independent tone-bearing unit (TBU). However, not every TBU is underlyingly specified for tone. Rather, the analysis for which we present evidence in this study recognizes two underlying tones /H/ and /L/ (high and low), which contrast with /Ø/ (absence of lexical tone). … /H/ varies between high and mid pitch, /L/ is realized on a level low pitch, and /Ø/ varies between level mid and falling low pitch.
tone_statements.locator: p.130 §1 (end) and §2, continuing on p.131; downstep p.145 §4; Tables 2-3 pp.141, 143.
tone_statements.summary: Three-way lexical contrast H vs L vs toneless Ø (surface mid or low-falling) on each vowel of the root couplet; L floating, one per root, on the stressed first vowel only; upstep and downstep.

tone_statements.summary: Two tone registers, high and low, in bisyllabic tonemic couplets (low-low, low-high, high-low, high-high), plus a 'tone modification' feature with lowering effect (high>mid, mid>low); after Daly.

High high, high low, and low low of a three tone system are the same tone patterns without modification in a two tone system.

sources.quote: Tone Bearing Units (TBUs) are syllables, and each can be H(igh), L(ow), or unspecified Ø. The evidence for underspecification is diverse. The specified tones H and L can form rising LH-contours, whereas Ø cannot form any contours. … Finally, the phonetic realisation of Ø is low-falling unless followed by H, in which case its pitch will match H. Neither the low-falling realisation nor the H anticipation are indicative of a phonological specification as M or another full-fledged tone.
sources.note: Syllable = TBU, each H, L or toneless Ø; rising LH contours are tone sequences; floating L docks rightward across words; OCP-L, H-tone spreading, floating-L deletion; data from Daly & Hyman 2007.

sources.citation: Daly, John P. & Larry M. Hyman. 2005. On the Representation of Tone in Peñoles Mixtec. UC Berkeley Phonology Lab Annual Report 1 (2005): 129-162 (page span per the PhonLab file name). doi:10.5070/P76X08707M;https://escholarship.org/uc/item/6x08707m
sources.quote: While the underlying system consists of a contrast between /H/, /L/ and /Ø/, pitch realization rules produce high-rising, low-falling, and mid output tones. … In PM each V is an independent tone-bearing unit (TBU). However, not every TBU is underlyingly specified for tone. Rather, the analysis for which we present evidence in this study recognizes two underlying tones /H/ and /L/ (high and low), which contrast with /Ø/ (absence of lexical tone). … /H/ varies between high and mid pitch, /L/ is realized on a level low pitch, and /Ø/ varies between level mid and falling low pitch.
sources.locator: p.130 §1 (end) and §2, continuing on p.131; downstep p.145 §4; Tables 2-3 pp.141, 143.
sources.note: Three-way lexical contrast H vs L vs toneless Ø (surface mid or low-falling) on each vowel of the root couplet; L floating, one per root, on the stressed first vowel only; upstep and downstep.

tone.quote: These languages are all tonal and tone carries a high functional load both in lexicon and grammar. … The tone-bearing unit (TBU) in Mixtec is the mora, which means that each ‘couplet’ has two tones. These two tones can be level or contour tones, depending on the variety. … All varieties except Peñoles, Coatzospam, Tepango, and Jicaltepec have a mid tone reflex for Proto-Mixtec *high, while the five mentioned varieties have a low tone reflex. … Most varieties have a low tone reflex, but Jicaltepec, Peñoles, and Coatzospam have a high tone reflex.
